content: Leptospirosis is an infectious disease caused by bacteria of the genus Leptospira. These bacteria are often found in water or soil that has been contaminated with the urine of infected animals. The disease can affect both humans and animals. Without prompt treatment, leptospirosis in humans can result in serious complications, including kidney damage, meningitis (inflammation of the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord), liver failure, respiratory distress, and even death. Globally, approximately one million cases of leptospirosis occur annually, with nearly 60,000 deaths reported. The disease has been documented across the United States as well. Humans and animals can contract leptospirosis through direct or indirect contact with contaminated urine or other bodily fluids, often via water or soil. Infected animals may exhibit a wide range of symptoms, or they may remain asymptomatic while continuing to shed the bacteria in their urine for months or even years. In humans, leptospirosis can present with a variety of symptoms, including fever, headache, chills, muscle or body aches, nausea, vomiting, jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes), red eyes, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and rash. These symptoms can mimic those of other illnesses, and some individuals may not exhibit any symptoms at all. The incubation period for leptospirosis ranges from 2 to 30 days following exposure to the bacteria. The disease may progress in two distinct phases. During the initial phase, individuals may experience fever, chills, headache, muscle pain, vomiting, or diarrhea. After a brief period of apparent recovery, some individuals may enter a more severe second phase, characterized by kidney or liver failure or meningitis. The duration of illness can vary from a few days to several weeks, and without treatment, recovery may take several months. If leptospirosis is suspected, it is critical to seek medical attention promptly for diagnostic testing and initiation of appropriate antibiotic therapy. The bacteria responsible for leptospirosis are primarily transmitted through the urine of infected animals. These bacteria can survive in moist environments, such as water or soil, for weeks to months. A wide range of animals, both wild and domestic, can carry the bacteria, including livestock (e.g., cows, pigs, horses, sheep, goats), dogs, cats, rodents (e.g., rats, mice), marine mammals (e.g., sea lions, seals), and other wildlife. Infected animals may not show any signs of illness but can continue to excrete the bacteria into the environment. Human-to-human transmission of leptospirosis is rare. Humans can become infected through various routes, including contact with water or soil contaminated with the urine or bodily fluids of infected animals, particularly after hurricanes, flooding, or heavy rainfall. Direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected animals or consumption of food or water contaminated with infected urine can also lead to infection. Certain activities increase the risk of exposure, such as water-based recreation (e.g., swimming, kayaking, canoeing, rafting), hiking, hunting, gardening, outdoor maintenance, and occupations involving close contact with animals or contaminated environments (e.g., veterinary work, dairy farming, butchering). Individuals experiencing homelessness or living in crowded shelters may also face an elevated risk of infection. The risk of leptospirosis increases significantly following hurricanes, heavy rainfall, or flooding. Floodwaters and rainwater can become contaminated with animal urine, spreading the bacteria to natural water sources such as streams. People may inadvertently come into contact with or consume contaminated water during these events. To reduce the risk of leptospirosis, individuals should avoid swimming or wading in water that may be contaminated with animal urine, particularly after natural disasters or heavy rainfall. Avoid direct contact with potentially infected animals, and cover any cuts or abrasions with waterproof bandages. When working or engaging in activities near floodwaters or potentially contaminated environments, wear waterproof protective clothing, shoes, or boots. For those participating in water-based recreational activities, research the area for known leptospirosis risks and take precautions such as covering wounds with waterproof bandages and wearing protective footwear. Individuals in high-risk occupations, such as veterinarians, veterinary staff, livestock farmers, dairy workers, animal control personnel, butchers, sewage and sanitation workers, military personnel, and first responders, should take additional precautions. These include frequent handwashing, using personal protective equipment (e.g., gloves, footwear, eye protection), cleaning and disinfecting surfaces and equipment, vaccinating animals against leptospirosis, isolating sick animals, and implementing rodent control measures in the workplace. Leptospirosis is treated with antibiotics, such as doxycycline or penicillin. Early administration of antibiotics is crucial and can prevent severe complications while reducing the duration of illness. In severe cases, intravenous (IV) antibiotics may be required. Prompt treatment is essential to mitigate the risk of serious outcomes and facilitate recovery.
